<reason>High-level debate on both sides. B built the stronger frame ("same business, same risks, same rules"; "protections in force beat protections in a draft") and honestly conceded reach limits while extracting A's toolkit concessions. But A won the technical core. B effectively abandoned the exchange prong after A's Q1 forced the "almost none" admission about tZERO/Prometheum, which A converted into the decisive closing question: in force for whom? On the surviving broker-dealer prong, A supplied a concrete mechanism — customer-protection/segregation rules key to securities and their cash, so Bitcoin balances sit outside — and B answered only at the level of examination and net capital ("the examiner sees it on the same page"), never restoring segregation or bankruptcy priority for the asset, the very protections B said FTX victims lacked. A also flipped B's wheat example to show the toolkit isn't proprietary to the securities box, defused the timing argument by noting the securities regime was in force throughout the FTX era and protected almost no one, and flagged Madoff twice without answer. A's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a real but minor execution cost; the substance survived. B's case ended narrower than the motion and more asserted than defended.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure Q1 asking how much volume tZERO/Prometheum actually trade, which extracted B's candid "almost none" and became the fulcrum of A's rebuttal and closing ("a rule nobody can operate under is not in force" — protections in a museum), neutralizing B's strongest timing argument.</best_rebuttal>
